metrics.note: repeat_interval 72000s (matching MAINTENANCE_INDEX_USAGE), not 604800: weekly did not survive contact with the reports. index-usage-report defaults to --days 3, so on four days out of seven its whole fragmentation section was empty - not 'no fragmentation', just no rows inside the window - and the same 3-day default is what the scheduled report uses. With from_hour 1 to_hour 6 the effective cadence is one run per night: 20h after a 02:00 run it is due at 22:00, outside the window, so it waits for 01:00. timeout 1800s, not 300: the SQL is already in the cheap LIMITED mode, but it still walks every index of every database, and on the largest instance here (~1.66 TB) it measured 749s on 2026-08-01 - 300s timed out there while every other target finished in seconds. 1800 is deliberate headroom over that 749s, because the scan grows with the database. APP-METRICS in data/app_commands.json must stay above this: it is the budget for the whole pass, and raising this alone would only move the kill from the query to the daemon - which is worse, since that kill takes every other metric in the pass with it.

metrics.note: Instance login inventory for the server-metrics report: one row per server principal with its roles, notable server-scope permissions and password age. Status is always OK on purpose - this is the list, and the alerting on the same principals belongs to SECURITY_LOGIN_HEALTH and SECURITY_FAILED_LOGINS. Exists because those two are exception-based and so can never answer 'who can connect to this instance'.

The other half of TOP_DISK_READ_SQL. disk_reads finds the SQL that hurts the storage; buffer_gets finds the SQL that burns the CPU, and on a well-cached instance those are different statements - a nested-loop join over cached blocks is invisible to disk_reads and is the usual reason a box is pinned at 100% CPU with idle disks. Status is always OK: an inventory of the current worst offenders, not a threshold.

An UNUSABLE index is not a slow index, it is an absent one: queries silently full-scan and DML on the table fails with ORA-01502. ALTER TABLE MOVE, partition maintenance and direct-path loads all produce it as a side effect without announcing what they broke. Checks dba_ind_partitions as well as dba_indexes, because a partitioned index carries its state per partition and reads N/A at the index level - looking only at dba_indexes misses exactly the indexes partition maintenance breaks.

report_policy._note: First run against a real instance (2.236, run 28781) found 76 objects already invalid in one application schema - 73 views, 2 functions, 1 procedure. That is a true finding and a real backlog, but it is a backlog: it stays exactly as it is until someone recompiles, so alerting on it would repeat every report cycle forever, which is the repeating-alert pattern this project deliberately stops. collect_only keeps every row in the store and in the inventory report while keeping it out of the warning/critical reports. Turn this off once a schema is clean, and a newly invalidated object after a release becomes the alert it should be.

metrics.note: INVALID stored code does not fail when it breaks, it fails when it is next called - ORA-04068 in the middle of a business transaction hours later. Grouped by owner and object type rather than one row per object: a failed release invalidates a whole schema at once, and 300 rows saying so is one finding, not 300.

TABLESPACE_FREE_SPACE answers 'is there room left'; this answers 'what used the room', which had no metric on any Oracle release. Status is always OK - size is not a fault. The value is the trend across runs: a segment that doubles in a week is visible in the stored history, while no single reading of it would justify an alert. Every six hours because a dba_segments aggregate is not free on a large dictionary.

metrics.note: A dictionary-managed segment that reaches MAX_EXTENTS fails with ORA-01631 while the tablespace still shows gigabytes free - so TABLESPACE_FREE_SPACE reports healthy right up to the failed insert. 8i-only by design; see the unsupported reason on the 9i+ variant.

report_policy._note: An inventory of several hundred rows per instance, all status OK - the same shape as MAINTENANCE_INDEX_USAGE, and kept out of the warning/critical reports for the same reason. It feeds the per-server index page.

metrics.note: Deliberately not an Oracle variant of MAINTENANCE_INDEX_USAGE. Oracle records no per-index usage unless each index is put into ALTER INDEX ... MONITORING USAGE, which is a change to the database rather than to the monitor; filing Oracle rows under the usage metric would fill a page with zero-seek indexes that look unused and are not - the reading that gets an index dropped and a report query broken. These rows state what Oracle can say without being asked to start recording: what exists, its size, whether it is still usable, and how old its statistics are.

variants.name: oracle_undo_not_applicable
variants.unsupported_reason: Automatic undo management replaces manually sized rollback segments from 9i on, so header contention is not a question the DBA can act on there.

metrics.note: Too few rollback segments for the transaction concurrency makes sessions queue on the segment headers: a general slowdown with no slow SQL to point at, which is the kind of incident that gets blamed on 'the database' for a week. The waits/gets ratio is the standard reading; shrinks and extends are in the message because a segment that repeatedly extends and shrinks back to OPTIMAL needs a bigger OPTIMAL, not more segments.

metrics.note: Half the cadence of the other two interval counters, and measured rather than assumed. Aggregating sys.dm_exec_query_stats scans the plan cache, and on one measured instance (86,400 cached plans, 70,109 of them with statistics) that scan exceeded the 60-second timeout three runs in a row on 2026-09-03 while the same query returned in 0.4 s once warm. A metric that fails every 15 minutes on one instance teaches its reader to ignore the metric, and one that holds a plan-cache scan open for longer is worse than a missing reading -- so the timeout stays at 60 s and the exposure is halved instead. The hour reading survives: two collections 30 minutes apart still fill it, and the page labels the span it actually measured. An instance where this keeps timing out has a plan-cache problem of its own ('optimize for ad hoc workloads'); until that is fixed, disable it for that target through metric_overrides.
